source_text:
καὶ ταύτης ἕνεκα
τῆς αἰτίας ὁ ζωοποιὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγος ἰδίαν ἐποιήσατο σάρκα τὴν θανάτῳ κάτοχον,
ἵνα κρείττονα καὶ θανάτου καὶ φθορᾶς αὐτὴν ἀποφήνας, παραπέμψῃ καὶ εἰς ἡμᾶς

τὴν χάριν. ὥσπερ γὰρ κατεβιβάσθημεν εἰς θάνατον ἐν Ἀδὰμ, οὕτως ἐν Χριστῷ τὴν
θανάτου παρωσάμενοι τυραννίδα, πρὸς ἀφθαρσίαν ἀναμορφούμεθα. 513 δʹ. Τοῦ
αὐτοῦ ἐκ τῶν κατὰ Θεοδώρου λόγου πρώτου. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος
ἄνθρωπος εἷς, καίτοι τῶν ἑκατέρων προσόντων ἰδιωμάτων πλείστην ὅσην ἐχόντων
τὴν διαφορὰν πρὸς ἄλληλα κατά γε τὸ εἶναι τοιῶσδέ φημι· ψυχὴ γὰρ ἑτέρα παρὰ τὸ
σῶμα· οὕτως ἂν νοοῖτο καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ πάντων ἡμῶν Σωτῆρος Χριστοῦ.
thought_title: Life-giving Word makes death-bound flesh his own to transmit grace
orientation: Cyril is closing his argument that the Word assumed flesh so that, having overcome death in it, he might pass that grace to us.
pass_a_gloss: And for the sake of this cause the life-giving Word of God made his own the flesh held fast by death, in order that, having shown it stronger than both death and corruption, he might pass on also to us the grace. For just as we were brought down into death in Adam, so in Christ, having thrust aside the tyranny of death, we are being refashioned toward incorruption. 513 d. Of the same, from the first book against Theodore. For just as from soul and body [there is] one man, although the properties belonging to each have as much difference as possible toward one another in respect of being such as this, I mean: for the soul is other than the body; so it would be understood also in the case of the Savior of us all, Christ.

choices.english: the flesh held fast by death
choices.why: κάτοχος means held or possessed; 'held fast by death' keeps the dative of agent and the sense that death grips the flesh.

choices.term: κρείττονα καὶ θανάτου καὶ φθορᾶς αὐτὴν ἀποφήνας
choices.english: having shown it stronger than both death and corruption
choices.why: κρείττων with genitive means stronger than; ἀποφαίνω means to show or declare, and the aorist participle keeps the temporal-causal force.
rejected: having made it superior to death and corruption
having declared it above death and corruption

choices.why: παραπέμπω means to send along or transmit; 'pass on' captures the transfer of grace from Christ to us.
The passive of καταβιβάζω means to be brought down or caused to descend; the aorist passive keeps the completed fall in Adam.
παρωθέω means to push aside or reject; the middle participle keeps the active role of believers in Christ.
The present passive of ἀναμορφόω indicates an ongoing process of being reshaped; 'refashioned' matches the glossary for ἀναπλασθῇ.

pass_b_english: For this reason the life-giving Word of God made his own the flesh that death held fast, so that he might show it stronger than both death and corruption and pass that grace on to us. Just as we were brought down into death in Adam, so in Christ we have thrust aside death's tyranny and are being refashioned toward incorruption. [513d. From the same author, from the first book against Theodore.] Just as a human being is one from soul and body, even though the properties of each differ from one another as much as possible in what they are—for soul is other than body—so it would be understood also in the case of Christ, the Savior of us all.

last_rejected.quote: from the first book against Theodore
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐκ τῶν κατὰ Θεοδώρου λόγου πρώτου
last_rejected.why: πρῶτου modifies λόγου (first discourse), not a separate 'first book'; it's 'from the first discourse against Theodore.'
last_rejected.fix: from the first discourse against Theodore
last_rejected.ruling: λόγος can mean 'discourse' or 'book/treatise'; both are within normal semantic range. No meaning changed.

last_rejected.quote: we have thrust aside death's tyranny
last_rejected.why: Greek is aorist participle, not perfect active; 'having thrust aside' or 'when we thrust aside' needed
last_rejected.ruling: Aorist participle παρωσάμενοι can render as 'having thrust aside'; English 'have thrust aside' conveys completed action adequately here.

last_rejected.quote: so it would be understood also in the case of Christ
last_rejected.source_quote: οὕτως ἂν νοοῖτο καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ πάντων ἡμῶν Σωτῆρος Χριστοῦ
last_rejected.why: Missing 'Σωτῆρος' as title; 'Christ, the Savior of us all' should be 'our Savior Christ' or 'Christ our Savior'
last_rejected.fix: so it would be understood also in the case of our Savior Christ
last_rejected.ruling: 'Christ, the Savior of us all' correctly renders τοῦ πάντων ἡμῶν Σωτῆρος Χριστοῦ; claim is mere preference.

problems.quote: pass that grace on to us
problems.why: Same action described with different verbs in summary and text.

variants.text: pass that grace on to us

problems.why: 'Thrust aside' is unusually violent and physical for spiritual transformation; may misrepresent Greek middle voice.

problems.quote: 513d. From the same author, from the first book against Theodore.
problems.why: This editorial/section marker appears mid-paragraph with no signal; reader may think it is part of Cyril's text.
problems.fix: Set off as an editorial note with brackets or a heading.

problems.quote: from the first book against Theodore
problems.why: This work is titled 'Fragments from Book Two Against Theodore of Mopsuestia,' but this note says 'first book,' which may confuse the reader about which book is being read.
problems.fix: Clarify that this fragment comes from Book One, not Book Two.

edits.old: and pass that grace on to us
edits.new: and transmit that grace to us

edits.old: we have thrust aside death's tyranny
edits.new: we have cast off death's tyranny

edits.old: 513d. From the same author, from the first book against Theodore.
edits.new: [513d. From the same author, from the first book against Theodore.]

edits.old: from the first book against Theodore

fixed: The glossary issue about 'pass that grace on to us' was addressed by standardizing to 'transmit' in the English.
The mistranslation issue about 'thrust aside death's tyranny' was addressed by changing to 'cast off'.
The speaker issue about the editorial marker was addressed by setting it off in brackets.
The wrong_scripture issue about 'first book' was addressed by clarifying it as 'Book One'.

problems.quote: Just as a human being is one from soul and body
problems.why: Analogy introduced without signal; could be Cyril, Theodore being quoted, or standard theological example.
problems.fix: Clarify this is Cyril's analogy for Christ's unity.

problems.why: 'Toward' suggests incomplete process; Greek eis likely means 'into' or 'for' incorruption as achieved state.
Three renderings for the Word taking on flesh; reader may miss unity.
problems.fix: Use 'was made flesh' or 'assumed flesh' consistently

edits.old: Just as a human being is one from soul and body
edits.new: For just as a human being is one from soul and body

fixed: The glossary problem about 'was enfleshed' does not appear in the current English text; the English uses 'made his own the flesh,' which is not one of the flagged renderings, so no change is needed.
